title: UNIX V7: finding your way
text: In the tested V7 guest, pwd prints the working directory, ls lists directory entries, and cat displays a text file. The shell and commands run in the guest; a browser terminal is only their input/output surface. Start with a listing before editing a disposable file. These examples were exercised in the project laboratory, not inferred from the currently selected terminal label.
question: Explain pwd, ls and the UNIX root directory to a beginner.
keywords: unix v7 ls pwd cat directories

title: RT-11: a different command environment
text: The project's owner-operated RT-11SJ V05.03 baseline accepted DIR and SHOW CONFIG. That is recorded evidence for that guest, not a claim that every RT-11 version has identical commands or drivers. Do not substitute UNIX command syntax by assumption. Confirm the running guest and consult its matching manual before writing files or changing devices.
question: Explain how an RT-11 session differs from a UNIX shell.

title: RSX-11M: command context matters
text: DEC's RSX-11M Beginner's Guide (June 1977), section 3.2.1, describes the Peripheral Interchange Program (PIP) and its /LI directory-listing switch. Its command language and file naming differ from UNIX. Identify the installed RSX version and command interpreter before adapting an example; this project has not qualified an RSX browser tutor session.
question: Explain PIP and why RSX examples should not be pasted into a UNIX shell.

title: 2.11BSD: terminals and vi
text: The laboratory's 2.11BSD media contains /usr/ucb/vi and /usr/ucb/more. /usr must be mounted before checking those paths. The guest TERM setting and the browser's terminal personality must agree. The project's vi workflow uses a disposable file, insert mode, Escape, :w, Ctrl-L redraw, :wq, and readback; the browser never rewrites the guest program.
question: Explain vi command mode, insert mode and TERM using a disposable file.
keywords: 211bsd 2.11bsd vi more term

title: Octal and PDP-11 instruction words
text: Octal uses digits 0 through 7. One octal digit represents three binary bits: octal 17 equals decimal 15. PDP-11 instruction words are 16 bits, often written in octal; an address radix must be stated explicitly. MOV copies a source operand to a destination using specified addressing modes. The device lab's MOVB polling programs exercise device registers; they are not OS printer drivers.
question: Work through octal 17 plus 1, then explain MOV versus MOVB at a beginner level.
keywords: octal mov movb instruction

title: Printer, paper tape and observation
text: Original SIMH owns LP11 and PC11 behavior. A device existing in SIMH does not prove a guest OS has its driver. Host-visible output may lag CPU writes because the simulator buffers files. Observation is read-only and requires explicit producer identity; an inactive browser does not imply a stopped CPU. PC11 reader input and punch output are separate media, and byte counts alone do not prove end-of-tape.
question: Explain printer spooling and the difference between a paper-tape reader and punch.
keywords: lp11 pc11 printer tape punch reader

title: PDP-11/70 address spaces
text: The PDP-11/70 uses 16-bit words and 8-bit bytes. A program uses 16-bit virtual addresses (64 KiB per address space); the memory-management unit translates them to 22-bit physical addresses. The 22-bit space spans 4 MiB, including reserved device space; it is not a statement that 4 MiB of RAM is installed. UNIBUS addresses are 18 bits. Separate instruction/data spaces do not make a virtual address wider than 16 bits.
keywords: pdp11 pdp-11/70 architecture virtual physical address addressing 16 22 memory
section: 1.6.1–1.6.3, printed pp. 1-7–1-8; digest of retained OCR text
question: Explain PDP-11/70 address spaces.

title: MOV, MOVB and addressing modes
text: PDP-11 operand specifiers contain a three-bit mode and three-bit register number. Register deferred (mode 1) uses the memory address in the register without changing that register. Autoincrement (mode 2) uses that address, then increments the register: two for a word, one for a byte, except R6/SP and R7/PC always increment by two. Autoincrement deferred (mode 3) fetches a word pointer and increments by two. MOV copies a word; MOVB copies a byte and sign-extends it when the destination is a register. Other modes include register, autodecrement, indexed and their deferred forms.
keywords: pdp11 mov movb instruction opcode modes autoincrement register deferred
section: 3.3.2 and 3.4, printed pp. 3-5, 3-8–3-9; 4.5.1 MOV/MOVB, p. 4-26; digest of retained OCR text
question: Explain MOV, MOVB and addressing modes.

title: REALCONS and physical controls
text: REALCONS exchanges console state with a panel server; SIMH still owns CPU execution. Reading a panel input can advance switch-edge state. A browser disconnect, RPC reply or HALT request alone does not prove that a CPU halted. START release and polling/crash cases remain unresolved; the Web Desktop has no production panel control.
keywords: realcons panel switches halt start cont load adrs physical
question: Explain REALCONS and physical controls.

title: SIMH device and console boundaries
text: SIMH is the emulator. Its operator monitor commands are distinct from commands entered at a guest login terminal. A dedicated guest serial line is not the GNU Screen operator console. Device support in SIMH does not establish which guest driver is installed. Do not infer guest identity from a reused TCP port; each terminal attachment needs an explicitly verified generation.
keywords: simh emulator monitor console dc11 dz11 restart generation
question: Explain SIMH device and console boundaries.

title: Tektronix graphics versus text terminals
text: Tektronix 4010 plotting uses control bytes and coordinate encoding, not VT100 cursor commands. The laboratory V7 graph/plot path produced actual 4010 output. VT11 is a separate display processor interface, not the Tektronix stream. A browser personality does not configure a guest terminal or change its TERM setting.
keywords: tektronix tek4010 4010 vt11 plot graphics terminal
question: Explain Tektronix graphics versus text terminals.

title: Terminal personalities and guest configuration
text: VT52, VT100 and VT220 have different control sequences and supported subsets. A terminal personality changes browser interpretation; the guest still needs compatible terminal settings. Full-screen applications depend on TERM and terminal capabilities. Echo and erase behavior can originate in the guest line discipline; changing browser rendering does not rewrite the application.
keywords: vt52 vt100 vt220 term terminal echo erase keyboard

title: Interrupt vectors and saved context
text: A PDP-11 interrupt vector contains two words: the new program counter, then the new processor status word at vector address +2. On the PDP-11/70 the service address is in Kernel virtual address space. The old PC and PS are saved on the stack selected by the new status. RTI or RTT restores PC and PS from the stack. A vector is not a single instruction word.
keywords: interrupt interrupts vector vectors rti rtt 1170-vectors
question: Explain Interrupt vectors and saved context.

title: Registers, stacks and processor status
text: R7 is the program counter; R6 is the stack pointer. The PDP-11/70 has two sets of R0–R5 and separate Kernel, Supervisor and User stack pointers. The processor status word selects the register set, current and previous modes and priority, and contains N, Z, V and C condition codes plus the trace bit. This is the /70 organization, not a claim that every PDP-11 has identical registers.
keywords: registers stack pointer status psw r6 r7 1170-registers
question: Explain Registers, stacks and processor status.

title: Autodecrement happens before access
text: For autodecrement addressing, -(Rn), the register is decremented before its contents are used as the operand address. In the handbook examples INC -(R0) decrements R0 by two before incrementing the addressed word; INCB -(R0) decrements R0 by one before incrementing the addressed byte. These R0 examples do not establish SP or PC special cases.
keywords: autodecrement decrement predecrement inc incb 1170-autodecrement
question: Explain Autodecrement happens before access.

title: UNIBUS and memory-mapped devices
text: UNIBUS carries address, data and control signals. Peripheral registers are assigned addresses and can be accessed with the same instruction mechanisms as memory. Transfers are asynchronous and interlocked: the receiving device responds to complete a transfer. Bus mastership can pass from the processor to another device such as a disk controller. This describes hardware organization, not a guest driver or permission to access host devices.
keywords: unibus asynchronous bus mapped registers 1170-unibus
question: Explain UNIBUS and memory-mapped devices.

title: V7 ls: listing and ordering
text: The UNIX V7 ls manual says a directory argument lists its contents and no argument lists the current directory. Default ordering is alphabetical. -t sorts by modification time, latest first; -r reverses the chosen ordering. -d lists a directory name rather than its contents. These are V7 options; GNU long options are not established by this source.
keywords: v7 listing ordering alphabetical v7-ls
question: Explain V7 ls: listing and ordering.

title: V7 shell redirection
text: In the V7 shell, < selects a file for standard input. > creates an output file or truncates an existing file to zero length. >> appends to an existing file or creates it if absent. Redirection can change guest files; use a deliberately chosen disposable path. These facts do not establish modern shell extensions or host-shell access.
keywords: v7 shell redirection append truncate v7-redirection
question: Explain V7 shell redirection.

title: V7 ed: entering text
text: In UNIX V7 ed, the a command appends text after the addressed line. Input ends with a line containing just a period. Text is edited in the buffer; consult the w command before expecting changes to be saved to a file. This is a line editor, not vi insert mode, and the example is for V7 ed.
keywords: v7 ed editor append buffer v7-ed
question: Explain V7 ed: entering text.

title: VT100 cursor positioning
text: In VT100 ANSI mode, CUP uses ESC [ followed by line and column parameters separated by a semicolon and final H. Defaults are line 1 and column 1. Line numbering depends on origin mode (DECOM). These are terminal protocol bytes; the guest TERM setting must match the selected terminal behavior.
keywords: vt100 cursor cup origin decom vt100-position
organization: Digital Equipment Corporation; transcription at VT100.net
question: Explain VT100 cursor positioning.

title: VT52 compatibility is a distinct mode
text: The VT100 manual distinguishes ANSI mode from VT52-compatible mode. VT52 direct cursor address uses ESC Y followed by row and column characters encoded with an offset of octal 040. ANSI CUP uses numeric parameters instead. A VT100 in VT52-compatible mode does not make the two protocols interchangeable. This source does not qualify a full VT220 implementation.
keywords: vt52 vt100 ansi escape protocol vt52-distinction
organization: Digital Equipment Corporation; transcription at VT100.net

title: SIMH disk and tape families
text: The SIMH PDP-11 manual distinguishes RK11/RK05 (RK), RL11 with RL01/RL02 (RL), TM11/TU10 (TM), and Massbus TM02/TM03 tape formatters (TU). They are different controller and media families, not interchangeable file suffixes. Simulator device support does not establish that an installed guest has its matching driver. This note is descriptive and supplies no media attachment or boot commands.

text: The RSTS/E V9.0 System User’s Guide describes HELLO or LOGIN followed by the User prompt for a PPN and then Password. Password characters are not displayed. LOGOUT and BYE end the terminal session; LOGOUT defaults to /FULL, with /BRIEF also available. Ending a login session is not a system shutdown procedure. These are V9.0 DCL instructions, not verified commands for every RSTS/E release or run-time system.

text: In the RSTS/E V9.0 DCL environment, DIRECTORY displays file information; TYPE displays an individual file’s contents. With no file specification, DIRECTORY lists the user directory on the public structure. The guide distinguishes file information from file contents. title: Deferred pointers and the stack pointer
text: @(Rn)+ is autoincrement deferred, mode 3: the register points to a word containing the operand address and advances by two, including byte instructions. @-(Rn) is mode 5: subtract two before fetching the word pointer. R6/SP autoincrement and autodecrement always step by two, including byte operations. In contrast, INCB -(R0) decrements R0 by one before access. The PDP-11/70 has three mode-selected R6 registers, with one active at a time.
keywords: deferred pointer stack autoincrement autodecrement r6 1170-deferred-stack

title: RSTS/E V7.0 keyboard monitors
text: RSTS/E V7.0 provides BASIC, RSX and RT-11 keyboard monitors: run-time systems interpreting commands within RSTS/E. Their names do not mean that the machine has booted a different operating system. They share system commands, while BASIC and RT-11 add environment-specific commands. Concise Command Language (CCL) lets an installation define additional commands, so local command availability depends on configuration. This description is for V7.0, not a V9.0 DCL procedure.
keywords: rsts rsts/e v7.0 basic rsx rt11 monitors runtime ccl rsts70-monitors

title: RSTS/E V7.0 terminal interfaces
text: The RSTS/E V7.0 product description lists DL11, DJ11, DZ11 and DH11 terminal interfaces and up to 127 terminals including the console. KL11, LC11 and DC11 are listed only for systems updating from Version 6C. Listed terminal types include VT52 and VT100. These are product capabilities, not evidence that a particular disk image was generated with a driver, that its lines are enabled, or that a browser terminal has been accepted.

title: RSX-11M-PLUS V4.6 password lifetime
text: The V4.6 release notes describe an account password lifetime of 0–127 days; zero disables lifetime checking. A separately set expired-password flag can still require a change; zero is not a promise that every expiration condition is disabled. Expiration forces a password change at a later login, with an explicit exception for batch jobs and virtual terminals. HELLO is the login task in this discussion. These are guest-account facilities, separate from browser authentication; a browser login does not log into the historical guest. This note does not authorize account changes.

title: RT-11 multiterminal support versus terminal sessions
text: The July 1984 RT-11 System Generation Guide permits multiterminal support in SJ, FB and XM monitors. It supplies programmed I/O for up to 16 terminals using DL11 or DZ11 interfaces; it does not by itself establish independent login shells. Applications must use the supported interfaces. This multiterminal configuration excludes VT11/VS60 graphics support. The same guide identifies DZ.MAC as the Professional-series RX50 diskette handler, not the DZ11 multiplexer driver. This earlier-edition reference is not proof that a particular V05.03 monitor was built with multiterminal support.

title: RSTS/E V7.0 generated terminal lines
text: The May 1979 RSTS/E System Generation Manual distinguishes hardware terminal interfaces from lines generated into the monitor. SYSGEN selects enabled line counts; a DZ11 has eight physical lines. Lines omitted during generation are treated as nonexistent and require regeneration before use. INIT SET can temporarily enable or disable already generated keyboards and modem controls; it cannot supply omitted terminal-driver code. A hardware inventory therefore cannot prove that a generated monitor can serve those lines.
